analysis.one_liner: Requires voter-verified paper ballots, post-election audits, and federal grants to secure election systems.
analysis.headline: The Election Security Act of 2019 was sent to six House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every voting system used in federal elections to produce a durable, voter-verified paper ballot that serves as the official record in recounts and audits, and would require audits designed to catch wrong outcomes. It would send roughly $1.4 billion in federal grants to states to replace noncompliant machines and run the audits, require voting machines to be made in the United States, and direct the Department of Homeland Security to share threat information with, and run vulnerability assessments for, state election officials.
analysis.who_benefits: Every voter in federal elections, whose ballots would leave a verifiable paper trail that controls in any recount or audit. Voters with disabilities would get a private, independent way to verify and cast a paper ballot, with dedicated research grants to improve access. States would receive federal money to replace old machines and conduct risk-limiting audits, and state election officials would get threat briefings, security clearances, and DHS vulnerability assessments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All federal voters, especially voters with disabilities

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal-election voting system to use an individual, durable, voter-verified paper ballot, makes the paper ballot the official record, and requires hand-counting in any recount or audit, with paper controlling over electronic tallies if they conflict

Requires that voters with disabilities be given an equivalent, private, independent opportunity to cast a voter-verified paper ballot, and authorizes $5 million in National Science Foundation grants to study and develop accessible paper-ballot verification for voters with disabilities, limited English, or literacy difficulties

Authorizes $1 billion for fiscal year 2019 plus $175 million in each of fiscal years 2020, 2022, 2024, and 2026 in grants to states to replace noncompliant voting systems, make security improvements, and adopt best ballot-design practices, and $20 million for states to conduct risk-limiting audits

Requires states to conduct risk-limiting audits — checks that statistically guarantee a wrong reported outcome is very likely to be caught and corrected from the paper record — and to publish reports confirming the audits were run properly

Requires voting machines to be manufactured in the United States and ballots to be printed domestically on recycled American paper, and requires election-infrastructure vendors to be U.S.-owned, disclose foreign sourcing, and report cyber incidents within three days

Directs DHS to share timely threat information with state election officials, expedite their security clearances, and run security risk and vulnerability assessments on request, and requires a pre-election threat assessment from the Director of National Intelligence before each federal general election

Requires the Election Assistance Commission to test certified voting hardware and software against the latest guidelines before each federal election and decertify systems that fail, treats electronic poll books as voting systems, and creates a voluntary bug bounty program to find vulnerabilities in election systems
Requires a national strategy and a bipartisan 10-member commission on protecting U.S. democratic institutions from cyberattacks, influence operations, and disinformation campaigns

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the roughly $1.4 billion in authorized grants plus $20 million a year for an innovation grant program. States take on new federal mandates for paper ballots, audits, and reporting, with some compliance costs likely exceeding the grants. Manufacturers of paperless electronic voting machines would lose that market, as their machines would have to be replaced, and election vendors face new testing, decertification, and incident-reporting rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes about $1.4 billion in voting-system grants plus $20 million a year in innovation grants through 2027, a substantial new federal expenditure on a function states have traditionally run and paid for
It imposes federal requirements on elections that states and counties administer, which states that prize control over their own election systems could resist as an overreach

It grandfathers some jurisdictions that used paper-record printers or certain ballot-marking devices in 2018, letting them delay full compliance until 2022, so voters in those places would not get full paper-ballot protection immediately
The Buy American and recycled-paper printing requirements and the mandated replacement of compliant-but-outdated machines could raise equipment and ballot costs for states and taxpayers
Participation in the bug bounty program is entirely voluntary for state and local election officials and election service providers, so the worst-guarded systems could simply opt out

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a verifiable paper record for every federal ballot, audits designed to catch wrong outcomes, and security support for state election officials — directly address well-documented weaknesses in U.S. election infrastructure. The costs are real but modest relative to the scale of federal elections, and the main honest objections are the federal mandate on state-run elections, the two-year grandfathering delay for some existing machines, and possibly higher equipment costs from domestic-manufacturing rules. On balance, a well-designed bill whose cost is the main trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever reported it back, and no floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi introduced the bill on May 10, 2019, joined by 24 original cosponsors

The same day, the House referred it to the Committees on House Administration, Homeland Security, Intelligence, Science, Space and Technology, Foreign Affairs, and Judiciary, with the timing of jurisdictional splits left to the Speaker

Over the next seven weeks it was referred onward to three subcommittees: Research and Technology, Cybersecurity, Infrastructure Protection and Innovation, and the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties subcommittee
The bill accumulated 54 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it
No committee ever reported the bill back to the House, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent election-technology vendors kept selling existing systems without the bill's paper-ballot mandate, Buy American requirement, testing and decertification rules, or three-day incident-reporting duty. States that would have faced the federal mandates kept full discretion over their election systems, and taxpayers did not fund the roughly $1.4 billion in grants. Voters who wanted a guaranteed paper record of every federal ballot got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Election-technology vendors and state election officials

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be read from sponsorship: all 54 cosponsors were Democrats out of 231 House Democrats, and none of the 197 House Republicans ever signed on.

industries.note: Makers of paperless electronic voting machines would have lost that market, since the bill requires replacement with voter-verified paper ballot systems by 2020 or 2022 and allows decertification of systems failing new cybersecurity guidelines. At the same time, the $1 billion-plus in federal replacement grants would have paid manufacturers to supply the new machines, while subjecting them to U.S.-manufacturing requirements, independent security testing, and three-day incident reporting.

industries.industry: Election technology and cybersecurity service providers
industries.note: State grants could be spent on vendor-supplied security services, vulnerability assessments, technical support, and electronic poll books, creating a federally funded customer base. In exchange, vendors would have to be U.S.-owned, disclose foreign sourcing, follow federal cybersecurity best practices, permit independent testing, and report cyber incidents within three days.

industries.industry: Domestic ballot printers and paper manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would require all federal-election ballots to be printed in the United States on recycled paper made domestically, guaranteeing demand for domestic printers and paper mills. The cost flows to states and ultimately taxpayers.

industries.industry: Foreign-owned or foreign-sourced election equipment suppliers
industries.note: The bill would bar non-U.S.-owned vendors from grant-funded work, require machines to be manufactured in the United States, and require disclosure of any foreign sourcing for parts, cutting foreign suppliers out of the federal-elections market.
